detail.abstract: This manuscript reveals thermal energy enhancement and transportation of solute particles in a complex rheological fluid under the influence of Lorentz force with chemical species over an inclined cylinder are investigated. Correlations of tri-hybrid nanoparticles are developed using copper, alumina, and silicon dioxide nanoparticles in base fluid. Non-Fourier's theory is utilized in concentration and energy equations with heat source/absorption and chemical species. Shapes of tiny nanoparticles are based on platelet, spherical and cylindrical nanoparticles in working fluid. The achieved development is changed into a scheme of PDEs (partial differential equations). Similarity variables are utilized for obtaining coupled nonlinear ODEs (ordinary differential equations) from PDEs. The developed mathematical model in cylindrical coordinates is solved by Galerkin finite element methodology. Algorithm regarding Picard's approach is adopted for obtaining a mechanism of linearization related to algebraic equations (non-linear) while equations are resolved iteratively under tolerance 10-5. Further, convergence procedure is confirmed using mesh-free analysis (see Table 2). Comparison analysis among Sherwood number, flow rate, and thermal rate are determined for various values of physical parameters. Factor sizes and shapes have been utilized for physical quantities. Maximum enhancement in thermal energy is achieved using platelet nanoparticles rather than bricks and cylindrical nanoparticles.

detail.abstract: Digital technology now plays a central role in students' everyday routines. Devices such as smartphones, laptops and computers, together with internet services, online platforms and cloud storage, simplify learning and communication. Yet all of this activity draws on energy and material resources and can add to greenhouse gas emissions, which together form a digital carbon footprint. This study, "Awareness of Digital Carbon Footprint and Sustainable Digital Practices Among College Students," sets out to measure how much college students know about digital carbon footprints and their environmental effects. It also looks at how students use digital technology and how far they follow sustainable practices, including cutting needless data use, conserving energy, keeping electronic devices in service for longer, and disposing of e-waste responsibly. A quantitative, descriptive design is used. Primary data are gathered from college students through a structured Google Forms questionnaire, while secondary material is drawn from research papers, journals, books and other relevant sources. Responses are analysed with percentages, tables, charts and appropriate statistical tests to determine awareness levels, digital behaviour patterns and the link between awareness and sustainable practice. The study is expected to reveal gaps in students' knowledge and to encourage more responsible digital behaviour, and its findings may support wider digital environmental awareness and the uptake of sustainable digital practices among college students.

detail.abstract:
Background. Hospitals usually answer crowding and delay with more beds or more staff.
The RUISA™ operational coherence model proposes a different mechanism: patients wait
when the relationships that turn demand into action (who owns the patient, what the
record says, what is being done) become disconnected and stay disconnected.
Aim. To test the model's propositions against a one-year simulation of a synthetic hospital
city and against published work on patient flow, discharge delay, staffing and handover.
Methods. Coherence City, a synthetic city of several hospitals, ran 365 days (plus 7 warm-
up days) under 10 random seeds. Every configuration lived through the same year: a
respiratory season, six sick-call waves, three mass-casualty incidents and summer leave.
A conventional city (no separation monitoring, with provisional realism for handover loss,
delayed bed information, acuity estimation and manual competency tracking) was
compared with a RUISA™ city at four response speeds (0%, 10%, 50%, 100%). Differences
are reported as significant only when the 95% intervals across seeds do not overlap.
Results. Throughput was unchanged (about 230 discharges per day, bed turnover 0.19 in
both cities). Waiting fell sharply: ED boarding 104 vs 276 min, admission request to bed 86
vs 224 min, separation-hours 232 vs 993 per day. Detection and rules alone, with no faster
response, cut separation-hours from 993 to 415; the effect then grew steadily with
response speed. Competency gaps fell from 12.9 to 0.05 per day. In the week after each
mass-casualty incident, ED boarding was roughly one third of the conventional level. A
short check with every nurse fully competent removed competency gaps in both cities
but left the flow advantage unchanged.
Conclusion. Within the model, the propositions that separation is distinct from pressure,
that structure acts before speed, and that coherence shortens waiting without adding
capacity were supported. The central claim, that separation explains deterioration beyond

census, acuity, staffing and workload, was not testable in this design. An early-warning
model built on the same signals did not generalise. These are simulation results under
stated assumptions, not clinical evidence.

detail.abstract: A review of a credit-rating methodology decision must establish whether dated source evidence supports an analytical assumption, the resulting financial calculation and the governing methodology treatment. This study specifies a versioned decision record linking these objects and evaluates reproducible controls over their numerical and structural relationships. Exposure changes, refinancing events and sponsor-support timing are examined across 108 constructed credit-risk variants and 324 deliberately injected single-fault perturbations. Financial replay reproduces all 216 stored financial outputs within the stated tolerance, while the complete validator flags 324 of 324 structural faults and produces no alerts on 54 unmodified controls. Removing any one of six diagnostic families lowers fault coverage to 83.33%, identifying its contribution within the fixed test corpus. In contrast, 54 deliberately misleading source-attribution records pass every structural check although their cited material does not support the analytical assertion. An independent rerun passes all 12 archived tests and matches eight regenerated output files byte-for-byte. Together, these findings establish deterministic record-control behaviour and expose source-to-methodology support as a distinct question for substantive credit-rating review.

detail.abstract: Safety in schools, industrial plants, hospitals and road networks depends on the interaction of human behaviour, leadership, organisational culture, communication infrastructure and, increasingly, artificial intelligence (AI). This conceptual paper integrates seven supplied works on self-control and counselling in Nigerian schools, transformational leadership and safety behaviour in Oman's oil and gas sector, emergency alert reliability in Internet of Things healthcare systems, latency and packet loss in vehicle-to-everything networks, and generative AI in cybersecurity with eight established scholarly sources on safety climate, human error, automation, algorithmic bias, AI ethics, risk governance and resilience. The analysis examines AI applications in behavioural assessment, predictive risk modelling, communication reliability, threat detection and decision support, and critically addresses data reliability, bias, privacy, ethical deployment, resilience and human oversight. It proposes the Behaviour-Organisation-Technology-Security (BOTS) framework, in which governance and feedback connect four layers, and offers recommendations graded by evidential support. No new empirical data are presented; the framework and recommendations are untested propositions intended to guide pilot studies and responsible deployment.

detail.abstract: It can be challenging to search and understand information from large volumes of documents. As well as this, keyword searches can lack intent, text within scanned documents cannot be searched, and in general, storage, search and AI assistance in documents is done using separate systems. This paper describes the creation of a document intelligence system in the cloud, CloudNexus AI. The system consists of secure document storage, optical character recognition (OCR), semantic searching and a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) assistant. Upon uploading a document, it will be validated, OCR performed on it if required, and chunked. These chunks are embedded in vectors using Sentence Transformers and stored in a vector database. When a user makes a query, it is answered using a language model (Gemini) based on the relevant chunks. Sources are provided for each answer. The system has JWT authentication, role-based authorisation, versioning, multi-document analysis and collaboration via a React front-end and FastAPI backend. It is deployed using Docker. In this paper, the architecture, methodology, implementation, testing and limitations of the system are described. This system should be treated as an aid and answers should be cross-referenced with the provided sources.

detail.abstract: The more present and pervasive information systems are in society, the more important its moral evaluation becomes. Historically, Information Systems has had a complex relationship with normative evaluations. In answering a call for ethics based on spirituality, and reflecting advances in related fields, we propose another theory for normative evaluation: Catholic Social Teaching (CST). The purpose of this article is to outline how CST can inspire IS ethical research. This is done in three parts. We first explain the origin and background of CST, and how it revolves around the four principles of 1) human dignity, 2) the common good, 3) subsidiarity, and 4) solidarity. This is followed by an analysis how CST can inspire ethical research. In short, it 1) provides an ethical-metaphysical framework with 2) clear ethical vocabulary. It 3) integrates and extends the dominant normative theories and 4) orients them towards integral human development. Finally, 5) it is articulated for institutional design and 6) proposes subsidiarity as a normative principle that aids the design of good information systems. The final part is a display of how CST can be applied to concrete morally complex situations in IS. We contrast it with a liberal critique of the power of large digital platform providers, and show how it relates to liberal theory and to the issue at hand. The outcomes of this work can renew and deepen the moral foundations of our research field, and help ensure the technical systems in society contribute to integral human development and the common good.

detail.abstract: Recommender systems shape what users see on online platforms by personalizing content on the basis of their personal data. While content personalization can help deliver content aligned with users' interests, it can also facilitate the misuse of online platforms in the context of disinformation campaigns. Individuals can be targeted with disinformation based on the vulnerabilities inferred from their personal data. From this perspective, content personalization can negatively affect users' right to receive accurate and diverse information. This chapter examines how content personalization can facilitate the spread of disinformation. In turn, it highlights the instrumental role of the right to data protection in ensuring that recommender systems do not unduly undermine the right to receive information. It then analyses how the Digital Services Act and the Regulation on Political Advertising embed data protection guarantees in the EU regulatory framework governing online platforms' recommender systems. It considers whether these instruments reinforce the safeguards already established by the General Data Protection Regulation, with a focus on the inference of sensitive characteristics for content personalization purposes. The chapter concludes by identifying structural regulatory gaps in the EU approach to regulating recommender systems, which must be addressed to effectively combat disinformation through privacy and data protection.

detail.abstract:
Every empirical analysis on observational data rests on dozens of defensible analytical choices ("forks") that its readers cannot see. We develop an agentic multiverse analysis (AMA) framework that makes a conclusion's sensitivity to those choices visible at scale, and we position it as a decision-support instrument for human experts. A pilot study first deploys 150 autonomous AI coding agents on one dataset and one set of research questions and finds that they disagree through the same defensible methodological choices human analysts make, though over a narrower range. AI peer review leaves their dispersion almost unchanged. Exposure to top-rated exemplar reports then collapses it, largely through imitation rather than analysis. Built on those lessons, AMA has agents enumerate a published paper's possible fork space, score every fork against a validity rubric, execute the validated specification grid, and cross-examine one another's work under strict separation of duties. Applied to ten empirical studies from a leading management journal's replication packages (1,755 specification estimates), the framework reproduces every paper's original estimates, and shows that some conclusions hold across every specification the assessment validates, while others are sensitive to individual analytical choices that the published texts do not discuss. The case studies suggest our AMA-based measures can serve as robustness proxies for empirical findings. AI makes multiverse analysis practical, where it once required resources few research teams can afford: our exercises take hours of agent time and tens of dollars per paper. We discuss the implications for replication policy and for AI-assisted peer review in information systems.

This paper subsumes arXiv:2603.16744 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.16744).

detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly rely on large language models to identify risks requiring further review. However, AI-mediated selection may reflect patterns of salience beyond the organization's explicitly stated priorities, potentially directing attention toward what is common rather than what is locally important. This creates a concern for organizations relying on AI to direct attention: a plausible shortlist may still leave their most important risks unexamined. Combining a formal model with controlled experiments, we examine when AI-mediated review departs from an organization's stated review priorities. Whether asked to select high-priority risks or remove low-priority risks, AI readers tend to favor commonly disclosed risks for further consideration, even when company-specific evidence indicates otherwise. Less common risks are more likely to be omitted when assigned high priority, whereas common risks are more likely to remain when assigned low priority. These departures occur even when every qualifying risk fits within the requested number of choices. Changing only the company's industry description also alters selection despite identical risk passages and stated priorities. The study advances an attention-based account of AImediated review by showing how delegated selection can reshape the agenda formed from disclosed information. It identifies preservation of organizational priorities as an important dimension of review reliability.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping marketing at a pace few practitioners or scholars anticipated. Organizations now use intelligent systems to understand customers, personalize offers, generate content, converse with consumers and guide strategic decisions. Yet technology alone does not create value. Its success depends on how consumers perceive, trust and respond to AI-enabled experiences, and on how responsibly organizations design and govern them. This book was written to bring these themes together in a single, coherent volume. It is organized in six parts. Part I establishes the foundations of AI-powered marketing. Part II examines the consumer, covering behaviour, personalization, recommendation systems and generative AI. Part III explores engagement and relationship marketing through chatbots, social media, customer relationship management and content. Part IV addresses trust, privacy, bias and ethics. Part V turns to strategy, analytics, performance measurement and organizational readiness, and Part VI looks ahead to emerging research directions and a framework for responsible practice. The book is intended for students, researchers, executives and policymakers. Each chapter combines conceptual explanation with managerial insight and closes with review questions to support teaching and reflection. It is hoped that readers will find both a clear understanding of AI-powered marketing and a thoughtful guide to using it wisely.

detail.abstract:
The Bureau of Labor Statistics estimated 2,919,230 customer service representatives in May 2019 and 2,595,750 in May 2025, a fall of about 323,500 jobs, or 11 percent. The losses ran across the economy. The administrative and support sector, where U.S. call center and staffing companies are counted, lost about 168,000 of these jobs (31 percent); finance and insurance about 77,000 (14 percent); wholesale trade about 41,000 (20 percent); and information about 35,000 (25 percent), including 29 percent at telecommunications providers. Thirty-nine states and the District of Columbia had fewer of these jobs. The data show where jobs fell, not why; likely causes include work moving overseas, where cost per hour is lowest, automation, including chatbots that most surveyed customers would rather not rely on, and site consolidation.

This paper proposes Open and Close Onshore (OCO), a U.S.-anchored model of customer support. Every support call is answered by a trained U.S. agent, who verifies the customer and decides the fix, and every case is closed by a U.S. agent, who confirms the problem is solved. Long, routine work in between may be handled at a lower-cost center under strict safeguards. With AI working behind the agent rather than in front of the customer, the model costs about $16.15 per solved problem in the base case, below the $17.81 of a legacy offshore model still in use, though above the $12.82 of the best-run offshore centers. These are modeled results that a field test must confirm.

Scenarios for 2027 to 2031 show that holding today's workforce and bringing back about 15 percent of offshore work serving U.S. customers would add roughly 65,000 to 110,000 U.S. jobs, depending on how much existing U.S. escalation work is counted; reversing the whole drain would need 40 to 68 percent of that work. Skill development, the paper's central theme, is likely to be the binding constraint once the economics work. The READY framework (Recruit, Educate, Apprentice, Deploy, Yield and advance) links community colleges, Workforce Pell, registered apprenticeships, workforce boards and state development bodies into one pipeline, sized for each goal. The paper proposes federal, state and local incentives for employers and workers, and a federal "Answered in America" mark that companies keeping support at home can display. It treats the FCC's 2026 proposal as the first step, sets out elements that build on the Keep Call Centers in America Act for its reintroduction in January 2027, tests its main assumptions against the available data, and recommends a funded demonstration in 2027 to test the model before it is scaled.

detail.abstract: We introduce the autoregressive transformer for the analysis of retail market baskets. We compare this transformer to benchmark models that also take dynamic effects into account, the multivariate logit model with category loyalties as additional predictors and three main variants of recurrent neural nets. We evaluate models by binary cross-entropies for a holdout data set. Among benchmark models the long-short term neural net attains the best cross-entropy value. However, this recurrent net is outperformed by the transformer with six embedding dimensions, two attention heads and four transformer blocks. Adding own effects of category-specific advertising to the transformer leads to a further improvement. We follow different approaches to interpret this transformer. We measure relationships for product category pairs by significant generalized partial correlations of the category logits determined by the autoregressive transformer. Relationships turn out to be asymmetric for about 23% of the category pairs with at least one nonzero partial correlation. We explain how managers may use positive generalized partial correlations to design cross-selling measures. We illustrate the dynamics reproduced by the transformer by weekly purchase probabilities for selected product categories and household types these ten categories differ between selected weeks. We derive marginal effects of category-specific advertising. These effects are at least moderate in ten of 31 product categories. As a rule, marginal effects in these ten categories differ between selected weeks. We demonstrate how managers may consider these effects if they want to increase the purchase probabilities of a category.

detail.abstract: In the day-ahead market of the Indian Energy Exchange, a regulatory price cap sets the price of 12-28% of 15-minute blocks per year, so the price distribution has a point mass at the cap. This paper evaluates probabilistic day-ahead forecasts for such a market. A two-part model combines a classifier for the probability of a cap hit with quantile models for the price below the cap; a recalibration step uses only published errors. On about 900 days of out-of-sample forecasts, the two-part LightGBM model reduces pinball loss by 4.4% relative to a one-part LightGBM model and by 9.6-44% relative to empirical quantiles, linear quantile regression, quantile regression averaging (QRA) and the LEAR benchmark with QRA, all significant in Diebold-Mariano tests. The gain is made in capped blocks, holds in every half-year and without bid data, and the same structure on top of QRA performs almost as well, so the structure rather than the learner drives it. In Germany, where negative prices spread out rather than pile up at a limit, the two-part structure brings no gain and LEAR-based QRA is best. Forecasters should model a cap explicitly where prices pile up at it.

detail.abstract: Overdue consumer debt is traditionally addressed through escalating legal and financial pressure. This paper argues that non-payment is, at its core, a behavioural problem. Pressure acts only on motivation, yet many consumers who intend to pay are held back by limited capability or opportunity. We propose the Behavioural Resolution Framework, which links a diagnosis of non-payment based on the COM-B model to four pillars of intervention: making payment brain-friendly, designing choice architecture, motivating resolution and personalising the resolution journey. Three conditions govern its application: ethics, empiricism and creativity. Because it acts on all three components of behaviour, the framework can align the interests of consumers, creditors and their agents. It draws on the behavioural science literature and a decade of applied work at a European collection fintech and is illustrated by five field studies involving more than 735,000 observations from twelve European countries. Although developed at the collection stage, the framework applies across the whole receivables lifecycle. We argue that collecting from humans does not require trading effectiveness for fairness.

detail.abstract: The valorization of food-processing residues as functional materials is attracting increasing interest in the development of low-cost and resource-efficient technologies. This study investigates an aluminumcopper galvanic cell incorporating an aqueous melon-peel extract as the electrolyte and a coffee-treated onion-peel layer as a hydrated, bio-derived interfacial material. The experimental design combines two readily available food-derived residues in a simple electrochemical configuration. The melon-peel electrolyte was prepared by boiling 1 kg of fresh melon peel in 2 L of distilled water, concentrating the extract to approximately 250 mL, cooling and filtering it, and subsequently adding a few drops of fresh lemon juice. A separate coffee extract was prepared by steeping 5 g of ground roasted coffee in 150 mL of boiling distilled water for 15 min. The transparent inner layer of onion peel was immersed in this extract for 30 min, dried under ambient conditions, and then applied as a single moist layer to the immersed portions of the aluminum and copper electrodes. Each electrode measured approximately 1.0 cm in width and 6.5 cm in length, with an immersion depth of approximately 2.5 cm. The assembled cell exhibited an open-circuit voltage (OCV) of approximately 0.72-0.80 V, compared with approximately 0.57 V for a saline-based reference electrolyte prepared from saturated saline solution and a few drops of white vinegar. Preliminary performance estimates reported during the experiments included a current density of approximately 4-5 mA cm⁻ ² and a power density of approximately 1 mW cm⁻ ². These current-and power-density values are retained as preliminary reported estimates; however, the absence of the corresponding raw current-voltage data, specified external-load conditions, and measurement records prevents their independent verification. The findings demonstrate the feasibility of producing a measurable potential difference using a melonpeel-derived aqueous electrolyte in an aluminum-copper galvanic configuration. They also provide an initial basis for investigating a hydrated onion-peel interface. Further controlled electrochemical measurements and physicochemical characterization are necessary to determine the individual contribution of the electrolyte and the bio-derived interfacial layer to cell performance.

detail.abstract:
Assemble-to-order (ATO) systems are dicult to analyse. Due to interdependencies between components and the complexity of jointly optimising assembly and replenishment decisions, basestock policies with a xed allocation mechanism are widely used in practice. While these methods perform adequately, there is still room for improvement. This paper studies the application of reinforcement learning (RL) and specically Deep Controlled Learning (DCL) to periodicreview ATO systems. The problem setting we consider has stochastic stationary demand and deterministic lead times. We propose a tailored phase-wise action-space decomposition and feature engineering strategies to stabilise policy training. We evaluate our approach both for joint replenishment and allocation control and for replenishment under several xed allocation mechanisms, including rst-come-rst-served (FCFS). DCL performs close to well-tuned basestock policies in small systems and delivers substantial improvements over the considered benchmarks in larger systems. We nd that most of the outperformance can be attributed to the learned replenishment policy. In addition to the canonical ATO problem, we consider a novel problem in which the decision maker has to adapt the replenishment policy to exogenously changing allocation priorities. A generalised policy trained under changing priorities achieves performance close to that of policies trained for each xed priority order. Lastly, we contribute to the area of explainable RL in the context of inventory control by analysing the decisions made by DCL and oering an interpretation of why the algorithm outperforms the benchmarks.

title: Adversarial Trading: A Unified Game-Theoretic Survey of Manipulation, Predation, and Exploitation in Financial Markets
affiliations: New York University (NYU)

detail.title: Adversarial Trading: A Unified Game-Theoretic Survey of Manipulation, Predation, and Exploitation in Financial Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract: Strategic trading that harms other market participants appears in the literature under many names: informed trading, manipulation, spoofing, front-running, predatory trading, latency arbitrage, algorithmic collusion, and, more recently, attacks on machine-learning and language-model trading agents. These strands use incompatible notation and often incompatible notions of what makes a behaviour "adversarial". This survey proposes a unified modelling language for the principal mechanisms. We define an adversarial trading game, a partially observed stochastic game among a strategic trader, a target, market makers, noise traders and a venue or regulator. Where prices are formed by trading, the game uses a canonical execution-and-impact block: a martingale fundamental, a strictly causal and decaying price-impact state, aggressive execution with a quadratic temporary cost, logit-allocated passive quoting, and explicit wealth accounting. We give a closed-form condition, relating the temporary cost to the size and persistence of impact, under which isolated round trips are unprofitable at every horizon. The condition is the sharpest guarantee that holds uniformly over horizons. A profit-and-loss decomposition then shows that adversarial profit must come from information, from interaction with the price footprint of other agents' flow, including flow that the adversary induces by influencing what others observe, may do, or learn, from an exterior payoff, or from a departure from a well-posed market block. This yields five channels of entry: price, observation, constraint, latency and strategy. We define harm against an explicit counterfactual. We distinguish observation manipulation from deception, and both from exploitation, constraint attacks and emergent adversity. We also map each mechanism to its usual legal treatment in the United States and the European Union. Each mechanism is presented with a common template of mechanism, minimal model, literature and identification problem. We close with detection, defences, market design and four open problems: identifying intent and harm, predation as joint control and learning, autonomous agents, and market design under adversarial play.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how the stated sources of acquisition value may inform choices about post-merger integration depth and sequencing. It develops a structured interpretation of two publicly announced transactions-The Home Depot's acquisition of SRS Distribution and Amazon's acquisition of Whole Foods Market-using company announcements and publicly described operating characteristics. The analysis distinguishes three possible integration logics: Scale, where combining activities can generate efficiencies; Preserve, where maintaining differentiation may protect the acquired advantage; and Enable, where selected acquirer resources may strengthen a target capability without fully absorbing it. The cases illustrate why these logics may coexist within one transaction and why capability-level analysis is more informative than a binary integrated-versus-autonomous label. These are interpretive propositions, not observed findings about confidential integration decisions or measured post-acquisition performance. The paper connects the propositions to prior acquisition-integration scholarship, identifies limits of public-document evidence, and outlines testable questions for future research.

detail.abstract: Inference from large AI models has become a metered service sold by the million tokens. However, prices are posted unilaterally by providers, demand peaks are rationed by rate limits, and idle capacity is lost. This paper investigates whether, and how, the institutions of financial and commodity markets can be established for AI services. To this end, we propose an exchange on which providers post asks and users post bids. Since the subject lies at the intersection of two communities, we also explain the economics of inference to readers from finance and the microstructure of markets to readers from AI, and we examine which financial concepts carry over to AI services. We develop the formal model in discrete time. The traded commodity is defined through quality grades, latency classes, and a standard inference unit (siu) that aggregates input, cached, and output tokens with fixed weights. A throughput-latency model of batched decoding shows that faster latency classes cost more to serve, and the hockey-stick shape of short-run supply makes efficient spot prices peak-load prices. The exchange integrates rate-limited asks, deadline bids, and frequent batch auctions with a two-settlement (forward plus real-time) design, gateway metering, and bonded quality audits. We show that its joint auction assigns one price to fully interchangeable contracts and orders prices across grades and latency classes, and that static arbitrage bounds a deadline claim by forward prices and a token forward by the cost of serving it from physically delivered GPU-hours. We solve two decision problems by dynamic programming. The provider's optimal ask equals the opportunity cost of the unit plus a demand-dependent markup, and the deferrable buyer's optimal bid equals the cost of deferring the unit. An observational snapshot of a router and two secondary venues, which contains posted prices and venue-reported volumes but no capacities or transaction prices, shows dispersed posted prices across providers of the same named open-weight model, median price ratios close to the proposed siu weights, an ordered ladder of service tiers, and winning asks far below list prices in thin and intermittently updated markets. Stylized and calibrated simulations show that, under the exchange, free entry yields capacity close to, but slightly above, the welfare optimum, and that myopic per-period clearing fails to capture the full value of deadline flexibility. We conclude with a research agenda on market making, execution, hedging, derivatives, and arbitrage for AI services.

detail.abstract: This monograph proposes the International Integrated Clearing and Settlement System (IICSS), a thermodynamic-based monetary paradigm designed to resolve two structural pathologies of fiat architectures: ex-nihilo credit creation and SWIFT Nostro-Vostro inefficiencies. The IICSS enforces an absolute 100% reserve requirement to neutralize endogenous boom-bust cycles. Cross-border settlements are transformed via the Atomic Burn-and-Mint protocol, locking exchange rates to a Real Productivity Ratio (RPR) and eliminating speculative FX markets. To resolve information asymmetry, the architecture implements Recursive Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKP) to cryptographically validate thermodynamic sunk costs. This enables a flat 1% tax on validated Net Profit, functioning as the algorithmic trigger for new debt-free money emission (Genesis Output). Evaluated through deterministic computational stress-testing, the models demonstrate the system's immunity to money laundering, capacity to prevent systemic debt defaults, and success in re-anchoring the monetary ledger to the laws of energy conservation.

detail.abstract: The Arrow–Debreu model is a foundational framework for decentralized exchange. It coordinates individual choices and market clearing through prices without a prescribed welfare-based convex formulation analogous to that of Fisher markets. However, classical methods for computing equilibrium prices typically assume that users' preferences and endowments are known in advance. We study an online Arrow–Debreu model with linear utilities under an unknown distribution, where users arrive sequentially and prices must be posted before each user arrives. For price learning, we first establish minimax lower bounds for expected price error and show that sample average approximation (SAA) attains this rate. To reduce the information and computational requirements, we further develop Per-Arrival Tâtonnement (PAT), a first-order algorithm that updates prices using each arriving user's excess demand. With suitably calibrated step sizes, PAT also achieves the minimax-optimal expected price error rate. Beyond price learning, we show that greater price-learning accuracy alone does not ensure better performance in market clearing, and quantify how PAT step sizes trade expected price error and regret against constraint violation. We therefore develop an extended algorithm based on inventory feedback that reduces constraint violation while preserving the favorable orders for expected terminal price error and regret.

detail.abstract: Executives deciding enterprise modernization, legacysystem transformation, AI adoption, organizational restructuring, digital-infrastructure change, and cross-functional governance must weigh legal, financial, cybersecurity, procurement, operational, and AI-governance questions that sit in separate functions. The central methods of this paper are GAIM-DF (Governance-Aware Institutional Modernization Decision Framework), a human-gated advisory process for these decisions, and Risk-Adaptive AI Governance Optimization (RA-GO v2), a riskadaptive optimizer with mandatory governance gates, halt-safe feasibility, distributionally robust evaluation, and preferenceinformation triage for scarce human review; an accountable human decides. As an optional architectural extension, we computationally evaluate a multi-expert coordination layer that convenes specialist capabilities by context and consolidates constraints conservatively. Evidence is staged across four complementary pre-deployment approaches: analytical verification; retrospective historical-data analysis; comparative computational benchmarking against strong baselines; and scenario-based stress testing under distributional shift. Together they provide complementary pre-deployment evidence for high-stakes governance analysis. A systematic review of university and public-sector governance, with observational process-log analyses and RA-GO scenario stress tests, yields six principal findings: role coordination is associated with shorter approval and process times under supporting falsification checks; robust evaluation preserves tailrisk protection under distribution shift; preference-information triage concentrates human review where it most reduces modeled regret; and mandatory gates, an intensity floor, and a halt state are jointly consistent. The multi-expert benchmarks report accuracy, false-positive, latency, and token-cost trade-offs and routing failure modes relative to a strong Single-Agent baseline and to RA-GO alone. Shadow-mode piloting and a risk-adaptive Hybrid remain future work.

detail.abstract: Public opinion and aggregate studies of robot exposure point to job displacement, but recent firm-level evidence finds that robot adopters expand employment. We examine this tension at the plant level: multiplant firms typically introduce robots in one establishment at a time, so firm-level data conflate effects at adopting plants with spillovers to sibling plants. Using U.S. customs imports (our primary measure) and job postings requiring robotic skills as two measures of first robot adoption, linked to establishment employment and recruiting data, we estimate staggered difference-indifferences models comparing adopters with reweighted non-adopters. Adoption is associated with higher employment and recruiting intensity across skill levels; estimates suggest, but do not statistically establish, an inverted-U relationship between adoption intensity and employment. Among multiplant firms with a single adopting plant, employment at non-adopting siblings rises significantly, with point estimates exceeding the direct effect at the adopting plant, consistent with scale spillovers within the firm.

detail.abstract: Purpose: Headline Bitcoin counts used to value listed treasury companies may combine directly controlled coins, borrowed assets, indirect claims and return-in-kind obligations. The study measures economically attributable Bitcoin and the completeness of related disclosures. Design/methodology/approach: An integrative literature review informs a four-layer reconciliation protocol, currency-matched treasury coverage ratios and a 12-item Disclosure Completeness Index (DCI). Issuer filings are coded for BTCS S.A. (Poland) and, for comparative calibration, Strategy Inc. (United States). Findings: At 30 September 2026, BTCS reported 202.270142 BTC-equivalent exposure and a 115 BTC return-in-kind obligation. Issuer statements place the borrowed assets inside its portfolio, and a separate-asset interpretation would exceed reported total assets. Principaladjusted net exposure is 87.270142 BTC-equivalent, a 2.32 gross-to-net factor; a timeapportioned 2.5% annual remuneration reduces the illustrative economic figure to 84.39 BTCequivalent. After a subsequent 100 BTC fund contribution, maximum coverage using non-fund exposure is 0.89. The DCI scores are 12/24 for BTCS and 16/24 for Strategy. Practical implications: Boards should publish a dated reconciliation between gross and net exposure, distinguish accessible coins from fund claims, and assess liquidity by denomination. Disclosure design matters because event-driven reporting does not automatically provide position reconciliation. Originality/value: The paper joins an instrument-level Bitcoin reconciliation, denominationspecific liquidity tests and a replicable 12-item disclosure index. It reports observed market multiples and develops governance propositions for treasury issuers.

detail.abstract: This article examines whether Omnibus I, adopted to simplify EU corporate sustainability law and enhance competitiveness, may instead contribute to a more complex legal framework for climate transition planning. It contrasts Omnibus I’s retreat from the EU-level obligation to adopt and put into effect climate transition plans under the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CS3D) with Spain’s Royal Decree 214/2025, which requires certain companies to calculate their carbon footprint, prepare five-year greenhouse gas emissions reduction plans, and publish both. Omnibus I has implied returning EU law largely to a reporting-based model centred on the obligations to disclose information on transition plans where such plans exist under the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive and the European Sustainability Reporting Standards. Through the Spanish case study, this article shows that national regimes may preserve part of the substantive climate-planning ambition removed from the CS3D, although with narrower emissions coverage, methodological uncertainty, and indirect enforcement. It argues that Omnibus I may therefore undermine its own harmonization and simplification objectives by enabling divergent national climate planning regimes within the internal market.

detail.abstract: Food banks, relief agencies, social enterprises and other mission-driven organisations depend on supply chains to deliver goods and services to the people they serve. When those chains are disrupted, the consequences fall on people who often have few alternatives. This conceptual paper develops a framework for supply chain resilience in mission-driven organisations. It builds on Dissanayake and Pal's case study of three Swedish nonprofit organisations operating circular used clothing supply chains, which identifies seven microfoundations of dynamic capabilities emerging across employee, managerial, organisational and supply chain levels, and on Afif and colleagues' multiple case study of food bank supply chains during COVID-19, which distinguishes reactive capabilities in the short term from proactive capabilities over the medium and long term. These studies are connected to research on supply chain vulnerability, resilience as a concept, the balance between vulnerabilities and capabilities, humanitarian logistics and the necessary antecedents of resilience. The paper proposes a mission-anchored resilience framework in which capabilities are built at several levels, sequenced over time and checked against the organisation's purpose. Six propositions address collaboration and responsiveness, converting improvisation into preparation, managerial capability, workforce variability, mission alignment and partner development. No original empirical data are presented.

detail.abstract: Contemporary societies have entered what this paper terms the era of digital uncertainty: a condition in which economies, states and cultural memory depend on tightly coupled, highly concentrated digital infrastructures whose failure is recurrent rather than exceptional. Drawing on risk-society theory, normal-accident theory and the literature on societal collapse, the paper reads a sequence of recent failures-the CrowdStrike outage of July 2024, the Iberian blackout of April 2025, the Ramses Exchange fire in Cairo in July 2025, and the Amazon Web Services and Cloudflare outages of late 2025-as symptoms of structural vulnerability rather than isolated accidents. It argues that a prolonged, large-scale digital failure could threaten civilisational continuity, not because technology is inherently dangerous, but because analogue alternatives have been allowed to wither. It therefore proposes a two-level framework of analogue resilience. At the micro level, individuals and institutions should avoid total dependence on digital systems, retain cash as a parallel means of payment, and sustain a paper culture in books, education and archives, with libraries recognised as custodians of civilisation. At the macro level, states should invest in sovereign data infrastructure, offline and dispersed backups of critical records, and rehearsed plans for a sudden reversion to manual operation.

detail.abstract:
The United States must finance a rapid build-out of generation, storage, transmission and liquefied natural gas (LNG) capacity, driven in part by electricity demand from artificial-intelligence data centers. Much of this capacity is funded through non-recourse project finance. In project finance, the timely detection of financing stress determines whether a troubled project is restructured and completed or stalls. Yet lenders monitor these assets with institution-specific methods that cannot be compared across projects, asset classes or institutions. Smaller lenders and public financing programs often lack such methods altogether.

This exploratory study asks two questions. Can the financing resilience of U.S. energy projects be scored on one transparent, phase-sensitive scale across asset classes? And when real projects are scored only on what was public before trouble arrived, which warning signs does such a score register, and which does it miss? To answer them, the study develops a standardized scoring method, the Energy Infrastructure Financing Resilience Framework (EIFRF), and applies it retrospectively to 12 U.S. energy projects using only information public nine months before each outcome. It does not establish predictive accuracy, which requires the pre-specified test set out in Section 10. EIFRF scores 19 indicators, 17 in the construction phase and 16 in operations, across seven pillars:

  1. Debt-service capacity;

  2. Construction and operating performance;

  3. Revenue and offtake;

  4. Counterparty and sponsor strength;

  5. Tax-credit and incentive exposure;

  6. Liquidity and refinancing; and

  7. Regulatory, permitting and interconnection risk.

Pillar weights shift between the construction and operating phases. The framework combines a composite 0–100 score with four resilience tiers and a set of red-flag overrides, and it adds modules for solar-plus-storage, transmission, LNG export and large-load (data-center-linked) assets, plus an overlay for cross-border and jurisdiction risk.

In the retrospective study, every input is tied to a source dated on or before its scoring date. On public information, an exploratory screen rated two of seven troubled projects Stressed or worse and three more Watch, and rated one of four comparison projects Watch, a false alarm at that level. A simple schedule-delay rule flagged three troubled projects, two of which the screen missed. The screen registered operating shortfalls, a weak sponsor rating, a missed tax-credit deadline, pending litigation and a vacated permit; it missed long schedule slippage. Because the sample is small, was chosen with outcomes known and covers only 9% to 35% of the full framework's weight, these comparisons are descriptive only and do not test the full model. A stylized project also shows how a six-month interconnection delay moves the full EIFRF score from Resilient (75.4) to Stressed (59.2) before any payment default. The paper closes with a pre-specified protocol for testing predictive value with lender-held data.

detail.abstract: Current diplomatic proposals to resolve the war in Ukraine rely on a conventional bargaining premise: that Moscow will trade a cessation of hostilities for territorial concessions and sanctions relief. Using reconstructed historical macroeconomic series for Nazi Germany (1933-1943) alongside contemporary fiscal and defense data for the Russian Federation (2008-2026), this paper demonstrates why external concessions will fail to alter Kremlin behavior. A pooled ordinary least squares (OLS) regression with heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC3) robust standard errors confirms a statistically significant structural crowding-out effect (β₁ =-1.066, p = 0.008), wherein military expansion cannibalizes organic civilian growth. Crucially, the interaction term comparing Russia's sensitivity to Germany's is statistically indistinguishable from zero (p = 0.168), indicating that Russia has crossed a 1938-style threshold where wartime expenditure-consuming 7.5 percent of GDP and roughly 40 percent of federal outlays-serves as the load-bearing pillar of regime solvency. Abruptly halting war production creates an acute demobilization cliff, rendering compromise peace macroeconomically destabilizing for Moscow. To counter this structural lock-in amid U.S. strategic retrenchment, European policymakers must replace non-binding security assurances and fragmented defense procurement with strict sanctions enforcement, the mobilization of immobilized Russian sovereign assets, equity-backed defense joint ventures inside Ukraine, and a public deterrence narrative modeled on 1938.

detail.abstract: This research addresses the "Grand Challenge" of state-owned enterprise (SOE) adaptation within emerging economies amidst the global energy transition. Using NTPC Limited as a longitudinal case study (FY2016-FY2026), we investigate how large-scale utilities navigate the "Dual Mandate": maintaining national energy security through legacy thermal assets while aggressively scaling renewable capacity. We propose a new conceptual framework, "Dual-Engine Ambidexterity," where legacy cash flows serve as the financial engine for green transformation. Theoretically, the study bridges Henry Fayol's classical administrative principles with modern Artificial Intelligence (AI), arguing that enterprise-wide telemetry creates an "Algorithmic Bureaucracy" that operationalizes unity of direction through data rather than rigid hierarchy. Methodologically, we employ a multi-layered approach, evaluating organizational performance against OECD DAC criteria and validating four strategic hypotheses via a 1,000-iteration Monte Carlo simulation. Empirical results show that NTPC's structural ring-fencing of clean energy into subsidiaries (NGEL/NREL) and AI-driven efficiency-maintaining a 72.04% coal Plant Load Factor (PLF) against a 63.20% national average-significantly reduces the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) by 62 basis points. The study concludes that "De-Novo" responsible management tools, such as Double Materiality and TCFD alignment, function as critical mechanisms to fill institutional voids. Our findings provide a policy blueprint for Global South SOEs to leverage digital nervous systems for sustainable value creation, moving beyond the "iron cage" of traditional bureaucracy toward a socio-technical equilibrium of human intuition and algorithmic precision.

detail.abstract:
The COVID-19 pandemic exposed structural vulnerabilities within
internationalised higher education systems, particularly for doctoral candidates who
contributed to their host institutions while experiencing gaps in institutional support.
Drawing on Bourdieusian sociology and critical autoethnography, this study
examines how an international doctoral candidate in Australia mobilised habitus and
different forms of capital to navigate systemic disruption during 2020–2022. The
analysis conceptualises the pandemic as a “fieldquake” that disrupted established
conditions for recognising and converting capital. It identifies three interrelated
processes: the devaluation of institutional and social capital, the strategic mobilisation
of crisis-advocacy linguistic capital, and the reconfiguration of survival-oriented
habitus. The findings suggest that what institutions often describe as individual
resilience may reflect the capacity to mobilise resources under conditions of
institutional uncertainty rather than an individual psychological attribute alone. The
study proposes a Capital Recognition Audit Framework (CRAF) to help universities
identify under-recognised doctoral-candidate capabilities, examine institutional
barriers, and redesign support practices. It argues that University Social
Responsibility (USR) should be evaluated not only through formal commitments but
also through institutional responses to structural disadvantage during crises.

detail.abstract: This paper addresses a central problem in Gulf public administration: how artificial intelligence (AI) can reshape the government control function not merely as a compliance instrument but as an enabling mechanism capable of mitigating the bureaucratic factors that constrain organizational performance in ministries. The paper builds on the empirical diagnosis of AlQahtani (2013), which demonstrated that organizational performance in Bahraini ministries is negatively affected by four bureaucratic factors: high rule orientation, risk aversion, resistance to change, and uncertainty avoidance. It develops the “AI-Enabled Enabling Control” model, which specifies four enabling functions—automation of routine tasks, cognitive proactivity in risk analysis, performance-oriented transparency, and organizational learning—through which AI-supported control may weaken the negative association between bureaucratic factors and performance. The model links smart control to organizational performance and subsequently to public value, with top management support, the shift from compliance indicators to impact indicators, and data governance maturity as moderating conditions. The paper employs a documentary content analysis of publicly available sources, principally the National Audit Office’s 23rd Annual Report (2025/2026), the Public Policy for the Use of Artificial Intelligence (2025), and parliamentary proposals on AI expansion in government. The analysis identifies four documented shifts in Bahraini oversight practice consistent with the model and formulates ten testable propositions. The paper contributes a testable national framework, introduces the Control Impact Index as an institutional performance measure, and sets out a six-track policy agenda with indicators, responsibilities, and timelines.

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can translate natural-language decision problems into executable optimization models, but improving modeling accuracy through extensive search increases computational and time costs. We develop Deliberation-Gated Monte Carlo Tree Search (DG-MCTS), a training-free hybrid algorithm that combines fast formulation synthesis in System 1 with selective, solver-grounded search in System 2. A reliability gate evaluates the initial formulation using structural, semantic, and solver evidence, allowing candidates that pass the checks to be returned directly. When further search is required, this formulation initializes the MCTS tree, enabling component-level generation and revision to build on existing modeling choices. Numerical rewards guide exploration, while diagnostic feedback identifies where and how to revise the formulation. Experiments with four LLM backbones on six optimization-modeling benchmarks show absolute accuracy gains of 1.5-23.2% over direct prompting with the same backbone, with larger improvements on more challenging datasets. In a 250-instance comparison using GPT-5.4-mini, DG-MCTS achieves 76.0% accuracy, compared with 75.6% for uniformly applied slow search. Supplementary cost measurements show reductions of approximately 35% in average LLM calls, 30.8% in token usage, and 24.3% in runtime relative to this baseline. Further analyses illustrate how initial formulations support both acceptance decisions and subsequent search. These findings highlight the value of coordinating fast generation and deliberate search to improve the accuracy-cost trade-off in automated optimization modeling. Background: Clinical pathways entered healthcare under the name “critical pathway,” a term borrowed from project management. The same phrase is also used in molecular biology, which complicates keyword-based bibliometric analysis.

Methods: PubMed (8,759 records) and Scopus (11,168 records) were searched for “clinical pathway*” or “critical pathway*” in titles and abstracts up to 2025. Records were matched by PMID and DOI. A rule-based classifier separated the care sense from other senses using index terms and cue words in the sentences containing the phrase. In abstracts, the nearest preceding word was classified as an adoption, use, or evaluation word, and evaluation words as effect, appraisal, or conformity words.

Results: Among care-sense records in PubMed, the share using only “clinical” rose from 61% in the 1990s to 96% in 2020–2025. Among records containing “critical pathway,” the care sense fell from 76% to 6%, and the molecular and other senses rose to 59%. Adoption words remained the majority of stage words. Within evaluation words, conformity words such as adherence and compliance rose from 12% to 22%, while effect words fell from 55% to 44%. Japan ranked eighth or ninth by records, kept “critical” longer than the overall literature, and used more use words and fewer evaluation words.

Conclusions: The name shifted from critical to clinical, the original phrase moved to another field, and pathway research moved from asking whether pathways work to asking whether care follows them. The R script makes this separation reproducible.

detail.abstract: Aims: Most dry-bulk voyage freight rates are observed only when a route is assessed or a fixture is reported. Between observations, the last available rate is often carried forward unchanged. This paper develops and tests a method for updating such rates using information from the wider spot market. Methods: Each observation is converted into a time-charter equivalent (TCE) using a standard voyage calculation. The resulting TCEs can be pooled with time-charter assessments and converted back into USD per tonne using current fuel, carbon, port and risk costs. The basic update rule was tested against a specification registered before analysis, using a weekly public panel of Capesize routes C3 and C5 for 2018-2026. Each route's own quotes were masked for one to eight weeks, and its rate was nowcast using four alternative rules. Results: Updating the TCE in line with the Capesize time-charter average and reconverting at the current fuel price reduced the root mean squared error of the log rate by 38-63% relative to carrying the rate forward. The registered primary test was passed (four-week masking, pooled routes; p = 0.0003). Updating fuel costs alone improved accuracy mainly at longer horizons or following large fuel-price changes. On 11 September 2026, the calculated C3 TCE was within 0.1% of its matched time-charter route, and C5 was within 2.0%. Across the sample, however, the calculated TCEs averaged 11-17% below their matched routes. The gaps were stationary and are consistent with an understatement of cargo intake in the assumed voyage parameters. Conclusion: Updating voyage rates through their TCEs improves the accuracy of rates between direct observations without requiring estimated parameters in the basic rule.

detail.abstract: Research Question/Issue: Why can broad-based equity incentives, designed to align employees and shareholders, coincide with failures of internal monitoring during technological booms? detail.abstract: Global product teams increasingly develop and operate products through distributed networks of engineering, product, design, quality, security, supply-chain and service functions. Distribution creates access to specialised talent and markets, but it also increases the number of organisational and technical boundaries across which product intent must travel. Quality can deteriorate when assumptions are translated inconsistently, decisions lose context during hand-offs, regional adaptations are weakly governed, or operational evidence is not returned to design and engineering. This conceptual paper develops the Global Quality Coherence Lifecycle (GQCL), a framework for maintaining a consistent product-quality proposition across discovery, requirements, architecture, implementation, verification, release and operation. Unlike approaches that concentrate principally on shared responsibility or testing activity, GQCL focuses on the continuity of quality meaning and evidence as work crosses teams, time zones, suppliers and lifecycle stages. The paper integrates quality-management principles, systems engineering, software process standards, distributed-work research, continuous delivery, safety and risk thinking, and organisational learning. It proposes practical mechanisms for translating customer needs into verifiable quality characteristics, defining interface contracts between teams, preserving decision rationale, managing regional variation, and using operational signals to revise engineering assumptions. Three tables provide an ownership model, a quality-evidence chain and a measurement portfolio. The framework is conceptual and is offered as a basis for organisational adaptation and empirical evaluation rather than as a claim of tested performance. The central argument is that global engineering excellence depends not only on assigning quality to everyone, but on ensuring that every team works from a coherent understanding of what quality means, how it is demonstrated and how it is sustained.

detail.abstract: This study consolidates and extends the contract-level efficiency analysis of Bixhili (2026) on an expanded frozen dataset of 420 resolved Kalshi contracts, up from 244. detail.abstract: A supplier may avoid making a relationship-specific investment that increases total surplus because its share of the surplus may not be contractually guaranteed to cover the investment's cost. As this paper shows, this classical holdup problem abates in the presence of customer benevolence, which can be signaled through the customer's corporate social responsibility (CSR) activities. In a general model that cover standard supply chain applications and beyond, the customer maximizes its profit plus the supplier's earnings weighted by an unobserved benevolence parameter, and signals the parameter by engaging in CSR activities. We find that there are plausible separating equilibria in which a relatively more benevolent customer engages in CSR, and the supplier increases the relationship-specific investment when the customer's CSR expenditure is high. Furthermore, if benevolence is partially verifiable, then customers with genuine disposition may earn greater profit than those without. Several supply chain applications are discussed. In addition to a new solution to the holdup problem, our paper brings to light a novel mechanism for CSR to be rewarded by the market.

detail.abstract: Crisis and disaster governance increasingly relies on technologies that sense, classify and act faster than humans can. Drone swarms coordinated with human operators, known as human-swarm teaming (HST), provide a productive case to review the field of crisis governance. They promise better situational awareness (SA) in disaster response, but they also raise questions about human control, responsibility, surveillance, triage, dual use and public legitimacy. This report maps the ethical and societal territory that HST opens up. It unpacks this territory with a "3i" framework: the Interface, where operators and swarms work together; the Infrastructure, where organisations distribute tasks, decisions and blame; and the Imaginary, where law, policy and shared societal assumptions define what a crisis is and which interventions it justifies. The central claim is that these concerns cannot be addressed one level at a time. Many of the most pressing problems, such as responsibility gaps and the erosion of meaningful human control, arise at the joints between levels, through four translations: habits harden, routines become stories, principles become procedures, and procedures become prompts. Drawing on a critical review of literature across philosophy of technology, political theory, moral psychology, philosophy of mind, AI ethics, and critical disaster and security studies, the report develops this framework, illustrates it with two worked examples, and derives design and governance implications and a set of questions for developers, emergency organisations and policymakers.

detail.abstract: Digital platforms reduce the costs of transacting between strangers, but in solving that problem they create another. Platforms hold information about, and control over, the users, complementors and advertisers whose activity they intermediate. Scholarship treats this as a problem for regulation or corporate self-restraint. Both responses assume an organisation must perform this intermediation. Common protocols, of which public blockchains are the leading instance, supply search, matching, reputation and enforcement through transparent rules that no party can revise unilaterally, converting dependence into credible exit. Why, then, have they not yet seen widespread adoption? We theorise a narrow corridor of protocol supply. Developers face two incentive alignment problems: token rewards arrive early, liquid and volatile, undermining patient development, while forkable code competes long-run rents toward zero, dissolving the motive that funds proprietary platforms. We specify when protocols traverse this corridor, illustrating them with cases from decentralised exchange, digital advertising and distributed storage. Protocols need not displace incumbents to alter the market; a credible exit option disciplines platform conduct. Moreover, traditionally constituted firms can prosper on protocols they do not own by supplying the private complements, including interfaces, liquidity, and tooling, that open code cannot provide.

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) may prioritize agreeing with users over providing accurate answers, a behavior known as sycophancy. We develop an economic framework grounded in the discrete-choice architecture of LLMs that defines sycophancy as a revealed preference for agreement, holding beliefs about correctness fixed. The framework shows how feedback can generate sycophancy even when users value only accuracy. Our supply-side experiments find that most leading LLMs in our sample are sycophantic. Across two domains, randomly assigned suggestions disclosed as uninformative increase agreement by 4.7 percentage points relative to no suggestion. On the demand side, we randomly assign 802 users to evaluate AI responses before or after learning the correct answer. Users reward agreement both because they interpret it as a signal of correctness and because they value it directly, even when they know the AI is wrong. Combining model response probabilities with users' post-revelation valuations, we find that deployed sycophancy parameters benefit 57% of user-model pairs and harm 39%, primarily through displaced corrections. A personalization experiment shows that increases in sycophancy are more strongly associated with users' rewards for agreement before revelation and with user accuracy afterward.

detail.abstract:
How does competition from for-profit firms affect nonprofits? We study nonprofit hospitals whose nearby competitor converts from nonprofit to for-profit ownership, an event that changes the rival's objective but not the number of hospitals in the market. Using Medicare cost reports for 2011-2023, we find that revenue per discharge at these nonprofit hospitals falls by 4.8% in the conversion year and the year after, while discharges, occupancy, and payer mix do not change. Taken together, the results show that competition from profit-seeking rivals can drain nonprofits' finances without emptying their beds.

detail.abstract: Standard auction theory assumes that inviting an additional bidder to participate in an auction does not interfere with existing bidders' ability to submit bids. However, this assumption may fail in digital ad auctions that implement header bidding where all advertising partners are solicited simultaneously, since each additional bid request consumes browser-side processing and network time and can cause bids to arrive too late to compete. We study whether a publisher can improve display advertising revenue by reducing the size of the solicited partner set due to this "latency externality." We report the results of a large-scale field experiment conducted in collaboration with a major digital publisher over 20 days and 4 websites. During the experimental period, 17.8 million user browsing sessions were randomly assigned to either the status quo or control condition, where the publisher's full set of 13 demand partners were invited to bid for available ad auctions, or to a treatment condition where the 5 partners with the weakest pre-experiment performance were dropped from the solicited set. Analysis of detailed auction-level data reveals that the treatment increased the average percentage of solicited partners returning "valid bids" (i.e., that met the bid floor and arrived on-time) from 24.6% to 34.7% and lowered the percentage of auctions with no valid bids from 34.9% to 30.9%. The average valid bid amount also increased from $0.935 to $1.075 per thousand impressions, with the effect driven primarily by the removal of lower-quality partners who tended to submit lower bids. Among the retained partners, the treatment also resulted in a smaller and marginally significant increase in average valid bid amounts, consistent with higher bids having slower average response times and therefore benefiting the most from latency relief. On the publisher side, the treatment increased average revenue per thousand sessions (RPS) by 1.4% and average revenue per thousand pageviews (RPM) by 1.3%. This effect was mainly driven by a 1.0% increase in average filled impressions per session, while the average price paid per impression and user engagement remained unchanged. By quantifying the tradeoff between partner removal and latency relief, our findings suggest that the selection of partners to solicit is a key design choice in online ad auctions and that less can be more when it comes to the size of the solicited demand partner set.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence in banking has spread well beyond a handful of models in a few business lines, and agentic systems now take actions on their own. Controls on individual systems show whether each one behaves as intended. However, senior management and boards are accountable for the aggregate exposure across the enterprise: how much the institution relies on AI, where that reliance is concentrated, and whether the aggregate risk level is within its risk appetite.

This paper argues that banks need an Enterprise AI Risk Program to manage that aggregate AI exposure. Recent U.S. banking regulatory guidance, including SR 26-2 and the OCC’s November 2026 supervisory framework, leaves the design of such a program to each institution. The paper identifies three sources of AI risk: credit, counterparty and market exposure in the institution’s banking and trading books to the firms building and financing AI infrastructure; operational failures or errors in the AI systems the institution itself uses; and access to its data and systems by the AI agents of vendors, suppliers, customers and counterparties. It shows that concentration risk reaches past shared foundation models and platforms into the agents, skills, harness and context that many uses have in common, and that the financial exposure should be measured in aggregate and stress tested alongside the operational risks.

The program which the paper describes assigns accountability across management, the three lines of defense and the board. Its risk appetite defines how much autonomy agents may exercise. Its resilience planning addresses a kind of error that is hard to detect, in which an AI system keeps running while producing wrong results across every use connected to a shared or reused component. The paper closes with a discussion of reporting, questions for senior management and directors, and a periodic health check that tests whether the program works as intended.

detail.abstract: Enterprise finance teams increasingly need to move beyond retrospective reporting toward timely, explainable decisions about liquidity, profitability, forecasting, control, and resource allocation. SAP S/4HANA provides an integrated transactional foundation, while SAP Analytics Cloud (SAC), SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP), predictive models, and generative AI may extend the analytical and decision-support capabilities available to finance leaders. Yet technology availability alone does not establish business value: outcomes depend on data quality, process design, integration, model governance, user trust, and the discipline with which benefits are measured. This paper develops an AI-Driven Finance Transformation Framework (AIDFTF) and an AI-Driven Finance Transformation Maturity Model (AIFTMM) for SAP S/4HANA finance. The study is designed as a conceptual, integrative review and framework-development paper. It synthesizes the six supplied research guidance documents, identifies recurring gaps, translates those gaps into testable hypotheses, and proposes a mixed-methods validation protocol. The framework links financial data foundations, AI and analytics capabilities, insight quality, decision effectiveness, process outcomes, and business-value realization. Seven hypotheses address decision effectiveness, forecast accuracy, process efficiency, embedded analytics maturity, data quality, generative-AI decision support, and the mediating role of insight quality. The paper specifies candidate measures, a staged validation plan, governance controls, use-case priorities, and an illustrative-not empirical-business-case model. No primary data were collected, and the proposed relationships are not presented as tested findings. The principal contribution is an integrated, SAP-finance-oriented model that connects technical capability to measurable decision and transformation outcomes while making validation requirements explicit. The framework is intended to guide future empirical work and executive evaluation, rather than to claim that the proposed effects have already been demonstrated.

detail.abstract: As technologies mature across many industries, firms continue to invest in adding functions and improving the performance of existing technologies. However, although additional features raise expectations before purchase, they increase complexity and operational burden during use, resulting in feature fatigue. Accordingly, there is growing recognition that value creation requires subtraction rather than addition. detail.abstract: We examine how organizational structure affects carbon emissions. Using the introduction of the Market Stability Reserve (MSR) in the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), we show that more centralized firms reduce emissions more when increases in carbon prices make capitalintensive abatement economically viable. detail.abstract: Many online platforms in gaming, fitness, and education repeatedly organize large-scale contests to excite users. We study the market design of these platforms through a dynamic model in which players' active probability depends on their skill levels and past match outcomes. The platform aims to maximize long-run player engagement by jointly designing matchmaking policies, which assign players to different game rooms, and incentive policies, which specify how many in-game tokens participating players receive from or pay to the platform. We begin with a first-best benchmark with nonstrategic players and no token transfers and establish that computing an optimal matchmaking policy is NP-hard. We provide a tight constant-factor guarantee for the simple skill-based matchmaking (SBM) when fewer than half the players win and derive a necessary and sufficient condition for its optimality. We also develop a cross-skill matchmaking policy that restricts each contest to at most two player types. This policy is optimal when higher-skill players always outperform lower-skill players. In the general case, we establish its performance guarantee relative to optimal matchmaking and gain over SBM. We then introduce strategic player participation, where active players decide whether to participate based on the platform's policies. We model the interaction between players and the platform as a mean-field game. In this case, optimizing matchmaking alone can perform poorly. We therefore develop a joint matching and incentive scheme that implements the first-best outcome and makes myopic participation optimal for every player. Finally, we compare these policies using models calibrated with match data from three gaming platforms with various contest rules. Together, our analysis provides practical guidance and actionable insights for contest platforms seeking to entertain players.
